strengths: The paper provides a genuine theoretical contribution: it proves last-iterate convergence to the (unregularized) Nash equilibrium of the two-player zero-sum game, whereas prior iterative methods (iterative IPO, SPPO, Nash-MD, INPO) only achieve average-iterate convergence or converge to a KL-regularized modified game that does not yield the robust-alignment (50% win-rate) guarantee. Theorem 1, Theorem 2 (linear convergence of the regularized solver), and Theorem 3 (convergence under approximate solutions) are non-trivial and carefully proved in the appendices.

The unification of diverse preference-optimization algorithms (PPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO) as implementations of the prox operator is elegant and practically useful: it lets COVAL be plugged in over existing methods as a black box with minimal change, which lowers the barrier to adoption.

The synthetic 3x3 intransitive-preference experiment cleanly isolates the phenomenon: it shows MD/iterative-IPO/SPPO cycling while COVAL converges to the unique Nash equilibrium in last iterate, providing crisp empirical support for the theory.

The paper is well organized, clearly written, and includes substantial appendix material (proofs, hyperparameter search, additional results), and the code/models are stated to be released, which supports reproducibility.

The LLM-based study goes beyond prior work by running up to 42 iterations (7 full passes over UltraFeedback), and the comparison tables (Table 2, Table 4) demonstrate that COVAL attains >50% win rate against every baseline and the best average, illustrating the stability benefit of repeatedly updating the reference policy.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. COVAL is essentially the conceptual prox-method / iterative-regularization scheme (Nesterov 2004; Nemirovski 2004) applied to the alignment game. The paper is transparent about this, but the core algorithmic idea is a known game-theoretic technique rather than a new mechanism, so the contribution rests largely on applying it and re-framing existing methods.

The evaluation protocol is questionable: the preference oracle used to generate pairwise training data (Llama-3-OffsetBias-8B) is also used as the evaluator. This creates a self-consistent/controlled loop in which the policy is optimized against the very model that scores it, so the reported win rates do not demonstrate generalization to real human preferences or to an independent judge. At minimum, an independent evaluator (e.g., GPT-4 or human judgments) should corroborate the ranking.

The empirical gains are modest and lack statistical grounding. In Table 2 COVAL scores only 50.00-55.90 against INPO-Small/INPO-Large and wins by ~1-3 points over other strong baselines; no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, so it is unclear whether differences exceed run-to-run noise.

Experiments are narrow: a single 1.5B model (Qwen2-1.5B), a single dataset (UltraFeedback), and no human evaluation or comparison to large-scale RLHF/PPO pipelines. No ablation isolates how much of the gain comes from the meta-algorithm versus from the underlying INPO sub-solver, and the COVAL-specific hyperparameter schedule (updating the reference policy when the first optimization step converges/overfits, switching eta^-1 from 0.002 to 0.01) appears tuned per-setting, raising reproducibility concerns.

The robust-alignment guarantee is a property of the exact Nash equilibrium; the practical algorithm only computes approximate solutions, and the paper reports a plain point where the objective can still fall short of the guarantee. Table 2 shows COVAL barely exceeding 50% in several pairings (50.00, 51.30, 55.16), which is within plausible noise and undercuts the strong framing of a strict >50% guarantee.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: the inability of the Bradley–Terry assumption, and hence of RLHF/DPO-style pipelines, to represent intransitive/general preferences, and the failure of existing MD-based self-play methods (iterative DPO/IPO, SPPO, INPO) to attain the exact Nash equilibrium of the alignment game.

The theoretical contribution is non-trivial and clearly beyond the state of the art: last-iterate convergence to the unregularized Nash equilibrium (Theorem 1), an extension to inexactly solved regularized games with accuracy t^{-4} (Theorem 3), and a linear-rate MWU result for the inner regularized game (Theorem 2, with a self-contained proof). Relaxing the 'bounded log density' condition to a support-matching assumption on the Nash equilibrium (Assumption 1) is a genuine improvement, and the proofs (Lemma 2, Corollary 2, Lemma 3, Lemma 4, Pinsker/three-point identities) are carefully executed.

The synthetic 3x3 intransitive game (Fig. 1a, 3, 4) is a crisp and convincing diagnostic: it clearly shows divergence/cycling of MD-style methods and the constant equilibrium gap of INPO (a KL-regularized solution), while CO... converges to the true Nash. This directly corroborates the theory and is the most convincing evidence in the paper.

The observation that a wide range of existing losses (PPO, GRPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, INPO, DRO, REBEL) can be interpreted as instantiations of the prox operator, and the resulting plug-and-play recipes (Algorithms 3–11), provides a useful unifying view and makes the method easy to adopt with minimal changes to existing pipelines.

The empirical study is substantial in effort (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, plus a 1.5B study in Appendix K; 18 iterations, ~100 A6000-GPU-hours per algorithm) and includes both a controlled oracle evaluation and a standard-benchmark sanity check (Table 3), reporting that no general capability is lost.

Comparisons are made against a sensible set of baselines, including the closest prior work INPO as well as Iter-IPO with tuned KL strengths; the paper is generous to baselines by reporting their best checkpoints (Table 1) and also reports final-checkpoint comparisons (Table 6) where CO... fares even better.

Positioning and related work are thorough and honest, including explicit discussion of concurrent/subsequent work (Wang et al. 2025, Zhou et al. 2025, Tiapkin et al. 2025) and a candid Limitations section about non-convexity, the lack of a provable guarantee in LLM practice, and the absence of a convergence rate.
weaknesses: The LLM-level evidence for the central 'general preference' claim is indirect. The preference oracle is a 50/50 mixture of two BT reward models (Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B and ArmoRM-Llama3-8B), which is a mild form of non-BT preference; no verification is given that the resulting pairwise preferences on the UltraFeedback data are actually intransitive, nor how large the intransitivity is. A demonstration with a genuinely intransitive or human-annotated preference signal (or a synthetic-but-realistic intransitivity injected into LLM training) would be far more persuasive.

Evaluation is self-referential: the model is trained to fit the oracle and evaluated against the same oracle on AlpacaEval prompts. The headline '>60.2% / >56.8% win rate against all compared algorithms' therefore measures agreement with the training oracle rather than genuine preference alignment. The only external checks (Table 3, GPT-4 judged AlpacaEval/Arena-Hard) show CO... essentially on par with baselines (e.g., Arena-Hard 41.3 vs Iter-IPO 43.8; AlpacaEval 53.5 vs INPO 51.6), and the paper concedes it loses to Iter-IPO on Arena-Hard. In other words, the practical payoff of unregularized-Nash convergence is not clearly demonstrated under an independent evaluator.

Theory–practice disconnect: Theorem 3 requires each regularized game to be solved to accuracy eps_t = O(c1^2/(9t^4)), which is far stronger than what is realized by the practical instantiation (only T=3 outer rounds, with the reference policy updated every 6 INPO iterations in the Llama runs). The asymptotic guarantees therefore do not explain the observed gains, and the paper offers no finite-iteration bound or diagnostic (e.g., measured duality gap or distance-to-Nash under the oracle) to bridge the gap.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported as point-estimate win rates with no confidence intervals, seeds/variance, or significance tests, yet margins over the strongest iterative baselines are moderate (60.25% and 62.98% against Iter-IPO in Table 1; 56.89%/57.89% against Iter-IPO/INPO in Table 2). It is hard to judge whether these margins are robust.

Fairness/comparability of hyperparameters: the tuning protocol differs across methods (e.g., eta^{-1} changed from 0.002 to 0.1 mid-training for CO... and for the 'long' baselines; baselines reported at their best checkpoint while CO... is reported at its final checkpoint in Table 1). While the paper argues this is generous to baselines, the resulting numbers mix 'best' and 'final' checkpoints and make the average column hard to interpret.

Novelty of the algorithm itself is moderate: the meta-algorithm is essentially the conceptual Prox-method / iterative-regularization proximal-point scheme with the reference policy updated to the latest iterate, which is close to existing iterative-DPO-style recipes and to concurrent work (Wang et al. 2025; Zhou et al. 2025) that also demonstrate last-iterate convergence in this setting. The authors' claim of being 'first' is hedged in a footnote and depends on the 'approximate solver' refinement, so the algorithmic advance is incremental relative to the well-established prox-method literature; the main contribution is the theoretical relaxation plus the practical recipes.

Minor presentation/consistency issues: e.g., Algorithm 9 states 'defined in Algorithm 6' where it should refer to Algorithm 8, and the appendix is dense enough that key practical guidance (how many outer rounds, how the reference-policy update triggers are chosen) is somewhat buried; no code/artifact link is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameter reporting.
